item.title: Gastrocnemius–Soleus Soft-Tissue Mobilization
clinicalUse: A walker reports calf tightness descending steps. Ask what happens during ankle dorsiflexion and stair movement before assuming that the muscle is physically shortened.
May be considered alongside exercise and load management when local muscular sensitivity contributes; assess vascular and tendon conditions first.
Compare weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion or a controlled step task.
patientPosition: Prone with ankle supported beyond the table if safe, or supine with the knee and lower leg supported.
Relax the calf and avoid aggressive end-range dorsiflexion during manual contact.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the leg with shoulders over the contact and wrists neutral; do not press directly on the Achilles tendon to 'find the calf'.
Keep access broad and supported so you can modify pressure immediately.
stabilization: Support the distal leg and ankle, keeping the knee comfortable and the lower limb from rolling.
Use a towel or pillow to avoid unnecessary pressure around the malleoli.
contact: Use broad palmar contact over the gastrocnemius muscle belly and, as appropriate, more distal soleus musculature.
Avoid the popliteal fossa and the deep neurovascular bundle, the Achilles insertion and any focal bruised area.
forceDirection: Apply slow longitudinal glide along the muscle mass or gentle cross-direction work within comfort, never forceful friction into a tender Achilles tendon.
Work proximally/distally as appropriate for the chosen contact; direction alone does not demonstrate improved blood flow or tissue remodelling.
dosage: Short, low-pressure trials of approximately 30–60 seconds per comfortable area can be used as teaching examples, not a fixed curative dose.
Use patient response to decide whether to continue; manual work should not displace progressive calf loading.
steps: Reproduce the chosen step-down or weight-bearing dorsiflexion task and note how it feels.
Screen swelling, redness, acute rupture signs, neurovascular problems, calf clot risk, bruising and skin integrity.
Support the lower leg in a comfortable position and obtain consent.
Make broad contact with the muscle belly while avoiding the popliteal fossa and tendon insertion.
Trial a slow, controlled, comfortable glide while monitoring sensation and guarding.
Stop immediately if pressure creates unexpected sharp pain, swelling-related concern or neurological symptoms.
Retest the same ankle/stair task and follow with progressive heel raises or mobility work when indicated.
reassess: Weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion and heel-rise comfort
Calf tolerance to relevant loading later in the day
mistakes: Trying to 'strip' the calf aggressively through pain.
Massaging a hot, swollen or unexplained painful calf without appropriate medical screening.
Attributing every change in dorsiflexion to a permanent tissue lengthening.
safety: Unexplained unilateral swelling, warmth, redness or calf pain needs medical evaluation for possible thrombosis; do not massage until assessed.
Do not manipulate over acute muscle rupture, infection, fragile skin or a recent bleeding injury.
Watch for altered sensation, vascular symptoms or significant pain escalation.
item.visualCue: Supported calf muscle belly → broad gentle glide, avoid popliteal fossa → test ankle dorsiflexion.

story.title: One staircase, two very opinionated calves
story.scene: A weekend hiker can climb stairs happily but descending brings a familiar calf tightness. The clinician first measures ankle dorsiflexion and checks the calf for concerning swelling or tenderness.
story.clinicalDecision: With the leg supported, broad contact follows the gastrocnemius–soleus muscle region in slow, comfortable strokes. The popliteal fossa stays off-limits. This is not a mission to 'strip' every muscle fiber.
story.retest: The same step-down is tested again. A more comfortable movement supports graded calf loading. If soreness increases or the step is unchanged, the trial may not be worth repeating.
story.punchline: Stairs make excellent examiners; they never read your technique certificate.
story.evidenceCaveat: Short-term comfort changes are plausible; a temporary sensation of softening does not prove permanent muscle length change.
